description: Team Expedition is a multidisciplinary team of aspiring scientists, developers, and problem-solvers participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge. We combine artificial intelligence, software engineering, and astronomical data analysis to develop innovative tools for exploring the universe. Through our SPHEREx Discovery Engine project, we aim to bridge the gap between complex astronomical observations and meaningful scientific discoveries. Making Space Exploration more accessible and efficient
summary:
Aphelion is a free web tool that lets anyone look through SPHEREx’s images of one patch of sky over time. You type in coordinates or pick a demo spot. The tool lines up every SPHEREx picture of that spot and plays them as a flipbook, so a dot that jumps between frames is easy to see. Compare mode shows a before picture, an after picture and the difference between them. Follow mode keeps an asteroid or comet in the centre while the stars slide past.

When you click something, the tool checks whether it is already known. It looks up asteroids and comets in SkyBoT, stars in Gaia and names in SIMBAD. It can also measure how fast a star moves across the sky, and we checked those numbers against Gaia. For Barnard’s Star we got 12.6 ± 2.6 against Gaia’s 10.4.

SPHEREx sees in 102 infrared colours, so the tool also asks what an object is made of. It builds gas maps of comets (CO₂ around 3I/ATLAS) and plots the colours of asteroids.

This matters because volunteers found most known comets and brown dwarfs, and SPHEREx sends far more data than scientists can check alone.
details:
What it does

Aphelion shows you how a piece of sky changes over time in SPHEREx images. You enter RA and Dec (degrees or hours), or pick one of the demo spots. The tool finds every SPHEREx image that covers that spot, cuts out the same small square from each one, lines them up north-up and plays them as a flipbook. Stars stay put. Asteroids and comets jump from frame to frame.

There are four views:

  • Wide view: one whole SPHEREx image you can zoom and drag.
  • Detail: the flipbook of a small box.
  • Compare: the first and last visit side by side, plus the difference between them, so slow movers stand out.
  • Follow object: pick an asteroid or comet and the tool keeps it in the centre while the stars stream past.

Click any dot and the side panel tells you what it is. Known asteroids and comets come from SkyBoT, stars from Gaia DR3, and names from SIMBAD. If nothing matches, it could be a candidate, and the panel tells you to check other frames before getting excited. Every view has its own link, so you can send someone exactly what you found.

The tool can also measure how fast a nearby star moves across the sky. We checked it against Gaia, SIMBAD and CatWISE and our numbers agree within 2σ (Barnard’s Star: 12.6 ± 2.6 vs 10.4).

What makes it creative

Lots of people have built blink viewers. SPHEREx is different because it sees in 102 infrared colours, and a moving object lands on a different colour in every frame. So we used that to ask what an object is made of:

  • Comet gas maps. We split frames into “gas colour” (CO₂ at 4.26 µm, CO at 4.67 µm) and “dust only” either side, then subtract the dust. For 3I/ATLAS this shows a CO₂ cloud around the comet, which matches what NASA’s own team published.
  • Asteroid type. We measure how much light an asteroid reflects at each colour. Stony asteroids have a dip near 1 µm and carbon-rich ones don’t. We tested it on 151 Abundantia (stony) and 24 Themis (carbon-rich) and both came out right.

How we built it

  • Python 3.12 with FastAPI for the server, astropy and reproject for the images, numpy and scipy for the maths.
  • Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in the browser, with no build step.
  • Data: SPHEREx images from NASA/IPAC IRSA (and the AWS open data copy as a backup), IRSA’s Moving Object Search Tool, JPL Horizons, IMCCE SkyBoT, ESA Gaia DR3, SIMBAD and CatWISE2020.
  • Hosted for free on a Hugging Face Space. No special hardware, just our laptops.
  • 144 Python tests and 101 JavaScript tests.

What we thought about

  • Don’t change NASA’s data. The only corrections applied to pixel values are NASA’s own: the flagged bad pixels and NASA’s model of zodiacal light. Everything else (brightness scale, hiding poor frames, invert) only changes how the picture looks and can be switched off. The “How it works” page lists each one.
  • Be honest about limits. NASA’s team saw water around 3I/ATLAS. Our simple method doesn’t, so the page says so instead of tuning until it shows up. Two test asteroids is a small test, and we say that too.
  • Don’t keep people waiting. NASA’s archive went down with errors during the hackathon. Demo spots now load from saved frame lists, and image downloads race IRSA against the AWS copy so whichever answers first wins.
  • Made for people who aren’t astronomers. Plain words, a guided tour and demo spots that show something moving right away.
